claims.text: Elevated-temperature exposure of pre-exposure Q235 steel promotes rapid formation of a dense, adherent, Fe3O4-rich oxide layer.
The elevated-temperature Fe3O4-rich layer suppresses corrosion degradation in chloride-containing environments relative to room-temperature exposure.
At room temperature, Q235 steel forms a less uniform oxide scale richer in Fe2O3.
Identically prepared, uncoated Q235 specimens should be compared in 3.5 wt.% NaCl at approximately 25 °C and 80–100 °C.
Temperature-dependent changes in oxide composition, thickness, and uniformity are the structural mediator of the proposed corrosion response.
Enhanced diffusion and oxidation kinetics at elevated temperature favor continuous Fe3O4-layer development.
An Fe3O4-rich layer is denser and more adherent than the room-temperature oxide mixture.
The dense, adherent Fe3O4-rich layer limits chloride-ion penetration into the underlying steel.
The room-temperature oxide is potentially porous and less protective, permitting higher corrosion rates.
Elevated-temperature specimens will develop a thicker and predominantly Fe3O4 oxide layer relative to room-temperature controls.
Elevated-temperature specimens will exhibit lower corrosion current density than room-temperature controls.
Elevated-temperature specimens will exhibit higher electrochemical impedance than room-temperature controls.
Temperatures above the proposed moderate range or thermal cycling may disrupt oxide continuity or adhesion and eliminate the protective effect.
Temperature effects on oxidation kinetics are generally well established.
Failure to obtain a more uniform Fe3O4-rich layer, or obtaining equal or worse electrochemical corrosion metrics at elevated temperature, would falsify the proposed protective-temperature mechanism.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as retaining its inherent surface properties, but the falsification design removes all initial surface oxides by pre-cleaning, so the tested surface may not represent the stated pre-exposure state.
